title: Hello, what's your name?
goal: Greet people, introduce yourself, and ask how someone is — and master the one verb that appears in nearly every Estonian sentence: *olema* (to be).
bekal: greet and say goodbye appropriately for the time of day
give your name, job, and origin with *olema*
ask yes/no questions with *kas* — and never mix up *ja* and *jah* again

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Esimene kohtumine
dialogs.intro: Budi has just arrived in Tallinn for a semester abroad. In a campus hallway he bumps into Kerli.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tere! Mina olen Budi. Väga meeldiv.
lines.id: Hi! I'm Budi. Nice to meet you.
lines.literal: hello! I am-I Budi. very pleasant.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.id: Nice to meet you. How are you?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Ka hästi. Kas sa oled siin uus?
lines.id: Fine too. Are you new here?
lines.literal: also well. is-it you are-you here new?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah, ma olen uus. Ma olen Indoneesiast.
lines.id: Yes, I'm new. I'm from Indonesia.
lines.literal: yes, I am-I new. I am-I Indonesia-from.

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Väga tore! Kas sa räägid eesti keelt?
lines.literal: very good! is-it you speak-you Estonian language-(partial)?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Thank you! But I'm still learning.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Jah, ma olen tudeng. Ja sina?
lines.id: Yes, I'm a student. And you?
lines.literal: yes, I am-I student. and you?

lines.speaker: Kerli:
lines.text: Mina olen õpetaja. Ma õpetan eesti keelt.
lines.id: I'm a teacher. I teach Estonian.
lines.literal: I am-I teacher. I teach-I Estonian language-(partial).

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Väga tore! Vabandust, ma pean minema.
lines.id: Great! Sorry, I have to go.
lines.literal: very good! sorry, I must-I to-go.

notes: ⚠️ **Ja is not "yes".** *Ja* means **and**; the word for "yes" is *jah*, with a *h* you really pronounce. This is the number-one trap for anyone who knows German or Scandinavian languages, where *ja* means "yes" — and it turns up right in this dialogue (*Ja sina?* versus *Jah, ma olen*). Hold a little breath at the end of *jah* and you won't get it wrong again.

**Mina olen** and **ma olen** mean the same thing. The long forms (*mina*, *sina*, *tema*) are used when you stress who you mean — notice Kerli uses one when introducing herself and when contrasting her job with Budi's. The short forms (*ma*, *sa*, *ta*) are used on all other occasions, and they are what you will hear most often.

**Kas** goes at the **front of the sentence** to make a yes/no question. The rest of the word order doesn't change at all: *sa oled tudeng* → *kas sa oled tudeng?* English has to flip the order ("you are" → "are you"); Estonian doesn't.

⚠️ **Language names are written in lowercase**, and they are noun + noun: *eesti keel* is literally "Estonia's language", not an adjective. The same goes for *indoneesia keel*, *inglise keel* (English), *soome keel* (Finnish).

grammars.title: Olema — the verb you will use most
body: Some languages drop "to be" in sentences like "I'm a student" (Russian, for one). Estonian **never** drops it. Every sentence like that needs a form of *olema*.
after: Notice rows three and six: **on** is used for both "he/she" and "they". There is no separate third-person plural form — one form does both jobs.
⚠️ **Tema/ta means both "he" and "she".** Estonian doesn't distinguish gender in pronouns, so there is no *he*/*she* choice to make — one less thing to worry about.

grammars.title: Mina or ma? Which one to use when
body: Every Estonian pronoun has two faces. The difference isn't polite versus impolite, but **stressed versus unstressed**.

head: Sentence
When it's used
rows: A normal sentence. The most common. Use this when in doubt.
Stresses "I" — for example to correct someone, or when introducing yourself for the first time.
"**He/she** is the teacher, not me." A contrast.

after: The rule of thumb in one line: **always use the short form**, unless you are contrasting or correcting. That is how native speakers talk.
There is one place where the long form is required: when the pronoun stands alone without a verb. *Kes on siin?* — *Mina.* (Who is here? — Me.) Answering *ma* there sounds odd.

head: Eesti keel
Say it
English
When
rows: All day, to anyone. The safest choice.
Somewhat formal; in shops and offices.
A greeting when meeting in the evening.
⚠️ Only when parting to go to bed.
The most common way to part.
A little warmer, for longer partings.
Casual, among friends. From Italian, just like "ciao".

blocks.text: ⚠️ Note that *tere õhtust* and *head ööd* **can't be swapped**. The first is for meeting, the second for parting — just like the difference between "good evening" on arrival and "good night" on leaving.

blocks.title: Asking how someone is
items: *Kuidas läheb?* — How are you? (literally: "how goes it?") The most common.
*Kuidas sul läheb?* — How are you doing? A bit more personal.
*Hästi, aitäh.* — Fine, thank you. *Väga hästi.* — Very well.
*Halvasti.* — Badly. ⚠️ Use it only if you really want to talk about it; Estonians answer honestly and will ask follow-up questions.

blocks.text: *Kas* is one of Estonian's biggest gifts to learners. It works like a spoken question mark: put it at the front and nothing else in the sentence changes — no flipping "you are" into "are you", no *do/does*.
To answer, *jah* or *ei* is enough. For a fuller answer, repeat the verb: *Kas sa oled tudeng?* — *Jah, ma olen.* / *Ei, ma ei ole.*

Other question words take the place of *kas* rather than being added to it: *Mis see on?* (What is this?), *Kes sa oled?* (Who are you?), *Kus sa oled?* (Where are you?), *Kust sa oled?* (Where are you from?), *Kuidas läheb?* (How's it going?)

head: Eesti keel
Say it
English
rows: Please. / Here you are. / You're welcome.

blocks.title: ⚠️ Palun does three jobs at once
items: **"Here you are"** — when handing something over: *Palun!* (Here you are!)
All three are the same word. Context tells them apart, and the context is never confusing.

blocks.text: The last phrase in that table is worth memorizing today. Estonians are used to switching straight to English when they hear a foreign accent; saying *ma õpin eesti keelt* is the politest way to ask them to stay in Estonian — and it almost always works.

vocab.en: please; here you are; you're welcome

Put the words in the right order.
